overview.text: William Shakespeare’s The Tempest is a romance and comedy organized around a shipwreck that Prospero, the exiled former Duke of Milan, stages through magic. On an island with his daughter Miranda, the spirit Ariel, and Caliban, Prospero directs the castaways’ movements, including those who helped drive him from power. Their arrival sets revenge and attempted conspiracies alongside theatrical spectacle and Miranda’s encounter with Ferdinand. The conflict ends with reconciliation, Prospero’s dukedom restored, and his renunciation of magic. The play stands out for its enchantments and morally complicated power relations: Prospero appears both wronged and controlling, while Caliban’s resistance raises questions about island ownership and colonialism.

key_facts.text: The earliest recorded performance was at court on November 1, 1611; the play may have been performed publicly before then.
The Royal Shakespeare Company identifies late 1610 or early 1611 as the likeliest time Shakespeare wrote the play, rather than a certain date.
The play was first printed in the 1623 Folio, after Shakespeare’s death.
Ariel helps carry out Prospero’s plans; at the end, Prospero grants Ariel freedom.
Caliban is the son of the island’s former ruler, Sycorax. Folger editors note that Prospero’s control of the island and Caliban invites readings about colonialism and resistance.
